headline: Untenshu is 運転 (unten) plus 手 (-shu).

sources.quote: 運転(うんてん) (unten) + 手(しゅ) (-shu)

examples.ja: 運転手は車の中で寝ていた。
examples.en: A driver was sleeping in the car.

headline: Oiwai is 御 (o-, polite prefix) plus 祝い (iwai, “celebration, a gift or present”).

sources.quote: 御(お) (o-, polite prefix) + 祝(いわ)い (iwai, “celebration, a gift or present”)

examples.ja: 御成功をお祝いします。
examples.en: I congratulate you on your success.

examples.ja: 心からお祝いを申し上げます。
examples.en: I offer you my hearty congratulations.

headline: Kanarazu is literally “not temporary”: 仮ならず (kari narazu), shifted via karunarazu.

sources.quote: /kari narazu/ → /karunarazu/ → /kanːarazu/ → /kanarazu/

Shift from 仮(かり)ならず (kari narazu), itself from 仮(かり) (kari, “temporary”) + ならず (narazu), in which the second element is the negative form of either the Classical Japanese copula なり (nari) or the verb なる (naru, “to become”). Therefore, the literal meaning is “not temporary” or “not becoming temporary”.

examples.en: I'll do it by all means.

headline: Muri is 無 (mu, “lack”) plus 理 (ri, “reason”).

sources.quote: From 無(む) (mu, “lack”) + 理(り) (ri, “reason”).

examples.ja: 彼の化けの皮をはごうとしたが、むりだった。
examples.en: I tried in vain to catch him out.
furigana: をはごうとしたが、むりだった。

examples.ja: 彼はどれだけ一生懸命やっても試験に受かるのはむりだろう。
examples.en: No matter how hard he may work, he will not be able to pass the exams.

headline: Hiru is derived from 日 (hi, “day”), plus an element ru of unclear meaning that 夜 (yoru) seems to share.

sources.quote: ⟨pi₁ru⟩ → */pʲiru/ → /ɸiru/ → /hiru/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *piru (“daytime”).
Derived from 日(ひ) (hi, “day”), suffixed with an element ru of unclear meaning. Compare 夜(よる) (yoru, “night, evening”), which seems to use this same ru element.

examples.en: She made her appearance around noon.
He sleeps by day and works by night.

headline: Mittsu is a shift from the previous 三つ (mitsu).

sources.quote: Shift from previous 三(み)つ (mitsu).

quotes: By surface analysis, 三 (mi, “three”) + つ (tsu, generic counter word).

examples.en: Tokyo Station is the third stop.

headline: Ha went /pa/ > /ɸa/ > /ha/, from Proto-Japonic *pa.

sources.quote: /pa/ > /ɸa/ > /ha/.
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pa. Cognate with Okinawan 歯 (hā).

examples.ja: その赤ちゃんは歯が生えはじめている。
examples.en: The baby is cutting his teeth.

headline: Ishi is likely cognate with 磯 (iso, “pebble; gravel; rocky beach”).

sources.quote: ⟨isi⟩ → /iɕi/
From Old Japanese. First cited in the Man'yōshū of 759. In turn, the Old Japanese is reconstructed as from Proto-Japonic *isoi.
Likely cognate with 磯(いそ) (iso, “pebble; gravel; rocky beach”).

quotes: The 石 spelling came about through customary use in Japan of this character for the unit of measure.

examples.en: Constant dripping wears away a stone.

headline: Hosoi was fososhi, then lost its shi ending and its medial k.

sources.quote: From Early Middle Japanese adjective 細(ふぉそ)し (fososhi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in き (ki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of い (i).

examples.ja: 彼は太っているくせに声は細い。
examples.en: His voice is thin even though he is fat.

headline: Chikara is a compound of 霊 (chi, “power, life force, essence”) plus 柄 (kara, “source, origin”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *tikara. Compound of Old Japanese elements 霊 (chi, “power, life force, essence”) + 柄 (kara, “source, origin”).

quotes: From Middle Chinese 力 (lik). The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing. Compare modern Cantonese reading lik⁶.

From Middle Chinese 力 (lì), but apparently from a different source dialect or at a different time than 力 (lik). The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing. Compare reconstructed Middle Chinese reading /li̯ək/ or Korean reading ryeok.
Only found in compounds and idioms in modern Japanese.

headline: San went */sam/ → /samu/ → /saɴ/, from Middle Chinese 三.

sources.quote: */sam/ → /samu/ → /saɴ/
From Middle Chinese 三 (MC sam|samH). Compare modern Mandarin 三 (sān), literary Hokkien 三 (sam), Cantonese 三 (saam¹).
In Old Japanese, this kanji was used phonetically to transcribe さむ (samu).
Borrowing from Mandarin 三 (sān), with the pitch accent different from etymology 1.

quotes: Likely an apophonic form of 六 (mu, “six”), compare 四 (yo, “four”) with 八 (ya, “eight”).

examples.ja: 私たちは一日に三回、犬に餌を与えている。
examples.en: We feed our dog three times a day.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Aka is Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *aka, and the source gives nothing earlier.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *aka.

meaning: (with te-form verb) please do for me
headline: Kudasai is the imperative of 下さる (kudasaru, “to give”), the honorific form of 呉れる (kureru).

sources.quote: Imperative (命(めい)令(れい)形(けい) (meireikei)) form of 下(くだ)さる (kudasaru, “to give”), the honorific form of 呉(く)れる (kureru). This form is said to have either directly shifted from an earlier 下(くだ)され (kudasare), which is more typical of 四(よ)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (yodan katsuyō, “quadrigrade inflection”) and its descendant 五(ご)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (godan katsuyō, “quintigrade inflection”), or to be a clipping of 下(くだ)さいまし (kudasaimashi) or 下(くだ)さいませ (kudasaimase), from 下(くだ)さり (kudasari, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 下(くだ)さる (kudasaru), then shifting from kudasari to kudasai in a process called イ音(おん)便(びん) (i-onbin, “-i sound shift”)) + まし (-mashi) or ませ (-mase), imperative forms of ます (-masu).

headline: Inoru is 斎 (i-, prefix expressing sacredness) plus 宣る (noru, “to say or express an intention, usually to a deity”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, first attested in the Kojiki (712 CE).
Derived from 斎 (i-, prefix expressing sacredness) + 宣る (noru, “to say or express an intention, usually to a deity”).

headline: Onaji is irregular even in Classical Japanese, mixing -i adjective and -na adjective behavior.

sources.quote: ⟨onazi⟩ → /onaʑi/
From Old Japanese.

An irregular adjective even in Classical Japanese (where the attributive form was usually 同じ), it has become more irregular in the modern language, mixing attributes of -i adjectives and -na adjectives (and sometimes neither).

quotes: The 未(み)然(ぜん)形(けい) (mizenkei, “irrealis”) and 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative”) form of two verb forms of the Sino-Xenic morpheme 同(どう) (dō, “same”).

examples.ja: おなじ間違いを繰り返すな。
examples.en: Don't make the same mistake again.

examples.ja: 始まりがうまければ半ばうまくいったもおなじ。
furigana: ばうまくいったもおなじ。

headline: Otoko may be おと (oto, “young?”) plus 子 (ko, “child”), compared with 少女 (otome).

sources.quote: ⟨woto₂ko₁⟩ → */wotəkʷo/ → /wotoko/ → /otoko/
From Old Japanese.
Derived from おと (oto, “young?”, cognate with Old Japanese 復つ (wotu → otsu, “to become young again”)) + 子(こ) (ko, “child”).
Compare 少(おと)女(め) (otome, “young woman”).

quotes: Compound of 男 (o, “male”, see above) + の (no, possessive particle) + 子 (ko, “child”).
The 呉音 (goon) reading, so likely the initial borrowing.
The 漢音 (kan'on) reading, so likely a later borrowing.

meaning: to hold, to carry; to possess
headline: Motsu is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, with cognates across the Ryukyuan languages.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *mətu.
Cognates

Cognate with Kikai 持ちゅい (muchui), Kunigami 持ちゅん (muchun), Northern Amami Ōshima 持と゚ぅり (muθuri), Okinawan 持ちゅん (muchun), Okinoerabu 持ちゅん (muchun), Southern Amami Ōshima 持ちゅむっ (muchum), Tokunoshima 持つぃ (mutsï), Yoron 持ちゅん (muchun), Miyako 持つぃ (mutsï), Yaeyama 持つん (mutsun), and Yonaguni 持とぅん (mutun).

headline: Jisho “dictionary” repurposes an older jisho meaning “letter of resignation”.

sources.quote: A repurposing of older term 辞書 (jisho, “letter of resignation”) (see below), based on a reanalysis of the constituent characters 辞 (ji, “resignation, quitting; word”) + 書 (sho, “writing, record, document, book”). Influenced by Middle Chinese-derived term 辞典 (jiten, “dictionary”), wherein the 辞 character expresses the meaning word from Middle Chinese 辭 /辞 (zi), instead of the meaning resignation or quitting from Middle Chinese 辤 (zi). Note that both of these older character forms were later conflated in both Japanese and Chinese into the simplified version 辞, with the word meaning becoming dominant in Chinese.

First appearance in Japanese with the dictionary sense might be the 1595 publication by the Jesuits of the 羅葡日辞書 (Ra-Ho-Nichi Jisho, “Latin-Portuguese-Japanese Dictionary”), alternate title Dictionarium Latino Lusitanicum, ac Iaponicum.
Compare modern Mandarin 辭書 /辞书 (císhū, “dictionary, lexicon”), possibly reborrowed from or otherwise influenced by the Japanese.
From Middle Chinese compound 辤書 /辤书 (zi syo, literally “quit + writing”).

quotes: The 直音表記 (chokuon hyōki, literally “straight-sound spelling”) of jisho above. Most common from the Heian through the Muromachi periods.
It is unclear if the pronunciation itself also shifted, or just the spelling.

examples.en: I will look it up in the dictionary.

headline: Kuni appears in the Kojiki of 712, and is perhaps related to Middle Chinese 郡 (“commandery”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Appears in the Kojiki of 712, the Nihon Shoki completed in 720, and the Man'yōshū completed some time after 759. Perhaps related to Middle Chinese 郡 (MC gjunH, “geographic region: commandery, prefecture”).

quotes: From Middle Chinese 國 (MC kwok, “country, nation”).

examples.en: He sold his country for money.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Hare is the stem of the verb 晴れる (hareru, “to be clear (of weather)”).

sources.quote: From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 晴(は)れる (hareru, “to be clear (of weather)”).

examples.en: I think it will be sunny.

meaning: expression of gratitude; thanking; gift of appreciation; bow
headline: Orei is 御 (o-, honorific prefix) plus 礼 (rei, “bow”).

sources.quote: From 御(お) (o-, honorific prefix) + 礼(れい) (rei, “bow”).

headline: Junbi is ultimately from Middle Chinese 準備, and attested from the early 1800s.

sources.quote: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 準備 (MC tsywinX|tsywet bijH). Attested from the early 1800s.

examples.en: I'm busy getting ready for tomorrow.

headline: Onēsan is 御 (o-) plus 姉 (nē) plus さん (-san).

sources.quote: 御(お) (o-) + 姉(ねえ) (nē) + さん (-san)

headline: Nakunaru is 無い (nai) in -ku form plus なる (naru): literally “to become not, to become nonexistent”.

sources.quote: The adverbial -く (-ku) form of adjective 無い (nai, “not, missing, not present”) + verb なる (naru, “to become”): literally, "to become not, to become nonexistent".
Cognate with 亡(な)くなる (naku naru).

headline: Amai was amashi in Early Middle Japanese, first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

sources.quote: From Early Middle Japanese adjective 甘(あま)し (amashi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in き (ki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of い (i). First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE. From Proto-Japonic *ama.

headline: Ban is from Middle Chinese 晚 (MC mjonX).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 晚 (MC mjonX).

examples.ja: 明後日の晩かえります。
examples.en: I'll come back the evening after next.

examples.ja: その晩は月が出ていた。
examples.en: There was a moon that night.

headline: Kare is 彼 (ka, “that, yon”) plus れ (-re); the male sense of “he” only arose later.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Compound of 彼 (ka, “that, yon”) + れ (-re, nominalizing suffix for demonstratives). Found in the Man'yōshū compiled around 759.

The sense development seems to have proceeded from "that thing over there" to "that person over there [of indeterminate gender]". The specifically male sense of "he" only arose later during the late Edo period and early Meiji period, influenced by translations of texts from European languages.

meaning: to carry out; to conduct (typically used in written language)
headline: Okonau may be おこ (oko, from 起く) plus なふ (nafu), though the source calls that suffixation unusual.

sources.quote: From classical 四(よ)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (yodan katsuyō) verb 行(おこな)ふ (okonafu), possibly formed from おこ (oko, from 起(お)く (oku)) + なふ (nafu, verb-forming suffix). However, the suffix なふ (-nafu) usually attaches on nominal roots, not other verb stems, making the theorized suffixation unusual.

examples.ja: 彼女の歓迎会を行った。
examples.en: We had a welcome party for her.

examples.ja: 大統領は大赦を行った。
examples.en: The president granted a general pardon.

headline: Shinpai can be analyzed as 心 (shin, “heart”) plus 配 (hai, “to concern oneself with”).

sources.quote: From the native Japanese word 心(こころ)配(くば)り (kokorokubari). Can be analyzed as 心(しん) (shin, “heart”) + 配(はい) (hai, “to concern oneself with”).

meaning: to leave, to go out; to appear; to attend
headline: Deru was idu: the initial i fell out in compounds, and du shifted to -deru only later.

sources.quote: ⟨idu⟩ → /id͡zu/ → /d͡zu/ → /d͡zuru/ → /deru/
From Old Japanese 出づ (idu), from Proto-Japonic *intu.
The initial i fell out in compounds where the preceding element ended in i. The du form on its own was not used much outside of compounds until the Kamakura period.

The ending then shifted from -duru (modern -dzuru) to -deru, a shift common to all 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs that occurred from the late Muromachi period through the early Edo period.
Some sources trace the development instead as ⟨idu⟩ → ⟨iduru⟩ → /id͡zuru/ → /d͡zuru/ → /deru/.

examples.en: You must go out of the room.

headline: Rei is from Middle Chinese 零, whose original meaning was a small rainfall.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 零 (MC leng) with an original meaning of a small rainfall.
For the modern sense of zero used since 1248 by mathematician Li Ye, see the Etymology section for Chinese for details.
